questions.title: Appraisal evidence
questions.prompt: Before planning a coastal passage, which inputs need to be checked? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Appraisal considers the vessel, navigation information and expected conditions, rather than treating a previous track as sufficient.
options: Draught, manoeuvring limits and available depths
The previous voyage track alone
Current charts and navigational warnings
Forecast weather and tidal conditions

questions.title: Passage planning responsibilities
questions.prompt: Match each passage-plan stage to its main task.
questions.rationale: The four stages have distinct functions; monitoring continues during execution.
definitions: Put the approved plan into operation
Develop the detailed route and limits
Gather and assess relevant information
Compare actual progress and conditions with the plan

questions.title: A changed passage plan
questions.prompt: A proposed route change introduces a new shallow-water leg. What should happen before using that leg?
questions.rationale: An altered route needs the same depth, hazard and operational assessment as the original plan.
options: Reappraise the risk, amend the plan and brief the bridge team under the ship’s procedures
Keep the original safety limits without checking them
Record the change only after arrival
Follow the new line as soon as it appears on ECDIS

questions.title: Position-fixing references
questions.prompt: Which features are generally suitable independent references for a coastal position fix? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Fixed, positively identified charted objects can support position lines; moving or unidentified targets cannot define a fixed reference.
options: A correctly identified fixed lighthouse
A moving ship on AIS
An identifiable charted radar-conspicuous headland
An unidentified floating object

questions.title: Light characteristic
questions.prompt: A chart labels a light Fl(3) W 10 s. What does the characteristic indicate?
questions.rationale: Fl(3) is group flashing with three flashes; W is white and 10 s is the complete repetition period.
options: One white flash every thirty seconds
A white light with three fixed sectors
Three different white lights ten miles apart
A group of three white flashes in a ten-second period

questions.title: Uncertain landfall
questions.prompt: At landfall, observed lights do not agree with the expected charted pattern. What is the best response?
questions.rationale: A mismatch is a reason to reassess the fix and safety margin before closing dangers.
options: Alter toward the brightest light to obtain a clearer view
Accept the electronic position without cross-checking
Assume the chart has changed and continue toward the coast
Treat the position as uncertain, verify it by independent means and call the Master as required

questions.title: Planning near offshore installations
questions.prompt: Which matters belong in a passage appraisal near an offshore wind farm? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The route must account for local restrictions, traffic and equipment limitations; a visual gap is not approval for a passage.
options: An assumption that every gap between turbines is an approved route
Current safety-zone information and local notices
Possible effects on radar observations
Support-vessel traffic and available sea room

questions.title: Joining a traffic lane
questions.prompt: When joining an IMO-adopted TSS traffic lane from its side, how should the vessel normally join?
questions.rationale: Rule 10 distinguishes a small-angle side entry from a right-angle crossing.
options: At as small an angle to the traffic flow as practicable
At a heading at right angles in every case
Against the traffic flow until clear of the boundary
By following the separation line

questions.title: Heading when crossing
questions.prompt: A strong current makes course over ground differ from heading. When crossing an IMO-adopted TSS lane, which should be as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general traffic flow?
questions.rationale: Rule 10(c) specifies heading; current can make the resulting ground track oblique.
options: The course over ground in every case
The relative bearing of the nearest ship
The vessel’s heading
The direction of the tidal stream

questions.title: Resultant ground motion
questions.prompt: A vessel heads due north at 10 kn through the water. A steady stream sets due east at 2 kn. Ignore leeway. Calculate true course over ground and speed over ground, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: East and north components are 2 and 10 kn. COG = atan(2/10) = 11.3°; SOG = sqrt(104) = 10.2 kn.

questions.title: Counteracting a northerly stream
questions.prompt: Required ground track is due east. Speed through water is 13 kn and stream is due north at 5 kn. Ignore leeway. Find true heading to one decimal place and speed made good to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: The water velocity needs a 5 kn southerly component. East component sqrt(13²−5²)=12; heading = 90°+asin(5/13)=112.6°.

questions.title: Starboard leeway
questions.prompt: With no current, the required track through the water is 090°T. Expected leeway is 4° to starboard of the heading. Which true heading should be steered?
questions.rationale: Heading 086° plus 4° starboard leeway gives water track 090°.

questions.title: Variation and deviation
questions.prompt: The required true heading is 137°. Variation is 5°E and deviation 2°W. Ignore leeway and current. Calculate compass heading in whole degrees.
questions.rationale: Compass error = 5°E−2°=3°E. Compass heading = true−east error = 134°.

questions.title: Gyro error from a transit
questions.prompt: A transit bears 058°T and simultaneously reads 060°G. What is the gyro error?
questions.rationale: True minus gyro = −2°, hence 2° west.
options: No error

questions.title: Changing gyro error
questions.prompt: A ship must maintain 100°T. Gyro error changes from 2°E to 4°W. What gyro course is now needed?
questions.rationale: True = gyro + signed error. With −4° error, gyro = 104°, an increase of 6° from 098°.

questions.title: Advancing a DR position
questions.prompt: A vessel steers 090°T at 12 kn through the water for 1 hour 30 minutes. Ignore current and leeway. How far east is the DR position advanced?
questions.rationale: 12 × 1.5 = 18 nautical miles east.

questions.title: Advancing a position line
questions.prompt: For a running fix in a known tidal stream, which motion should be used to advance the earlier position line to the time of the later observation?
questions.rationale: Advancement represents vessel movement over the ground, incorporating current and leeway as applicable.
options: The later compass bearing alone
Only the water-log distance, ignoring the known stream
The movement of the observed shore object
The vessel’s estimated ground displacement between observations

questions.title: Plane sailing triangle
questions.prompt: A short passage has difference of latitude 36 nautical miles north and departure 48 nautical miles east. Use plane sailing. Find course to one decimal place and distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Distance = sqrt(36²+48²)=60; course = atan(48/36)=53.1°T.

questions.title: Parallel sailing distance
questions.prompt: A ship travels east along latitude 60°N through 1°30′ of longitude. Use distance = difference of longitude in minutes × cosine(latitude). Find distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: 90 minutes × cos 60° = 45 nautical miles.

questions.title: Mercator sailing data
questions.prompt: For a north-easterly rhumb-line passage, difference of longitude is 160′, difference of meridional parts 120 and difference of latitude 72′. Use tan(course)=DLo/DMP and distance=DLat/cos(course). Find course and distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: tan C =160/120, so C=53.1°; cos C=.6 and distance=72/.6=120 nautical miles.

questions.title: Arrival across time zones
questions.prompt: Departure is 2300 on 8 June at UTC+3. Passage duration is 10 hours. Destination time is UTC−5. What is the local ETA?
questions.rationale: Departure is 2000 UTC on 8 June; arrival is 0600 UTC on 9 June, or 0100 at UTC−5.
options: 1700 on 8 June
2300 on 8 June
0100 on 9 June
0900 on 9 June

questions.title: Required average speed
questions.prompt: There are 84 nautical miles remaining and 7 hours until the required arrival time. What average speed over ground is required?

questions.title: Taking over the watch
questions.prompt: Before accepting the bridge watch, which matters should the relieving OOW understand? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: An effective handover establishes the navigational situation and applicable instructions.
options: Position, planned track and nearby dangers
Traffic, weather and the status of navigation equipment
Standing orders and any specific instructions
Only the name of the outgoing OOW

questions.title: Master on the bridge
questions.prompt: The Master arrives on the bridge without announcing a transfer of the con. What should the OOW assume?
questions.rationale: The Master’s presence alone does not constitute an understood transfer of responsibility.
options: The OOW retains watchkeeping responsibility until clearly relieved and this is mutually understood
Bridge records can stop until the Master leaves
Responsibility transfers automatically on the Master entering
The lookout may be dismissed immediately

questions.title: Compass error from azimuth
questions.prompt: A celestial observation has already been fully corrected to a true azimuth of 095.5°. The simultaneous compass bearing is 091.0°. Enter compass error as positive for east and negative for west, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Compass error = true bearing−compass bearing = +4.5°, or 4.5°E.

questions.title: Steering failure communication
questions.prompt: The rudder no longer follows bridge commands. Which actions belong in the immediate bridge response? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Steering failure needs immediate coordinated assessment and the established contingency response.
options: Use the ship’s emergency steering and communication procedures
Maintain lookout and assess traffic and navigational danger
Wait for the next routine log entry before reporting
Call the Master and advise the engine room

questions.title: Bridge record timing
questions.prompt: Why should the time of a significant course alteration be entered accurately in bridge records?
questions.rationale: Accurate timing supports navigation monitoring, handover and reconstruction of events.
options: To replace the need to record position
To allow the vessel’s movements and decisions to be reconstructed reliably
To avoid checking the next waypoint
To prove that no collision risk existed

questions.title: Ice blink
questions.prompt: What is ice blink?
questions.rationale: Ice blink is an optical indication of ice beyond direct view; it does not establish an exact ice edge.
options: A reliable AIS identification of every iceberg
A radar signal that always distinguishes ice from rain
The navigation light used by an icebreaker
A pale reflection from ice on the underside of low cloud

questions.title: Freezing spray precautions
questions.prompt: With freezing spray accumulating, which actions should be considered under the Master’s assessment? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Ice accretion calls for reduced exposure, stability awareness and safe working precautions.
options: Send unprotected crew onto an unsafe deck immediately
Adjust course or speed where safe to reduce spray exposure
Control access to exposed decks
Monitor the extent of ice accumulation and its stability effects

questions.title: Neap tide alignment
questions.prompt: Neap tides generally occur near which lunar phases?
questions.rationale: Near quarter moon, the solar and lunar tide-producing effects oppose in part, reducing range.
options: New and full moon
First and third quarter
Only the December solstice
Only the March equinox

questions.title: Overhead clearance reference
questions.prompt: A bridge clearance is charted as 30.0 m above HAT. HAT is 4.0 m above chart datum and current tide height is 2.0 m. A vessel’s air draught is 31.0 m. Ignoring all other allowances, find current bridge clearance and clearance above the vessel, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Bridge underside is 30+4=34 m above datum. Current clearance=34−2=32 m; above vessel=32−31=1 m.

questions.title: Water over a drying rock
questions.prompt: A rock has drying height 1.4 m above chart datum. Tide height is 3.9 m. Ignoring wave action, how much water covers the rock?
questions.rationale: Water depth = tide height−drying height =3.9−1.4=2.5 m.

questions.title: Rising-tide curve
questions.prompt: Use the training tidal curve. Low water is 0200 at 1.0 m; high water is 0800 at 5.0 m. What is the height at 0400? Give one decimal place.
questions.rationale: 0400 is 2 hours after LW. The plotted rise fraction is .20; height=1+.20×4=1.8 m.

questions.title: Time to reach a tidal height
questions.prompt: Use the training tidal curve. Low water is 0200 at 1.0 m; high water is 0800 at 5.0 m. When does the rising tide first reach 4.2 m?
questions.rationale: Required fraction=(4.2−1)/4=.80; the curve reaches .80 at 4 hours after LW, or 0600.

questions.title: Reduction of a sounding
questions.prompt: A sounding is 12.7 m below the water surface after all instrument and transducer corrections. Tide height is 2.3 m above chart datum. Reduce the sounding to chart datum.
questions.rationale: 12.7−2.3=10.4 m below chart datum.

questions.title: Vessel limits in appraisal
questions.prompt: Which vessel-specific information should influence passage appraisal? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Vessel dimensions and manoeuvring characteristics constrain the usable route.
options: Air draught where overhead restrictions exist
The vessel’s paint colour as the primary limiting factor
Turning and stopping characteristics
Loaded draught and required under-keel margins

questions.title: Contingency planning
questions.prompt: Why identify abort points and alternative anchorages while planning?
questions.rationale: Contingencies give assessed alternatives when limits or conditions are not met.
options: To prepare safe options if the intended passage cannot be continued
To guarantee the voyage will never be delayed
To permit any anchorage to be used without checking depth
To avoid briefing the bridge team

questions.title: Planning and monitoring tasks
questions.prompt: Match each task to the most relevant passage-planning stage.
questions.rationale: Information assessment precedes detailed planning; execution implements the plan and monitoring checks its progress.
terms: Mark no-go areas and clearing limits
Set the agreed bridge team for a restricted leg
Compare successive fixes with the planned track
definitions: Monitoring
Execution
Planning
Appraisal

questions.title: Sector light boundary
questions.prompt: A sector light changes colour earlier than expected during approach. What should the OOW do?
questions.rationale: Sector indications must be interpreted against charted limits and independent position information.
options: Continue regardless because sector boundaries cannot change
Check position and the charted sector limits and reassess the safe track
Assume the new colour proves the vessel is on the centreline
Use the colour change as a substitute for all position fixing

questions.title: Light height and range
questions.prompt: In a light description Fl W 10 s 25 m 15 M, what does 15 M indicate?
questions.rationale: Capital M denotes the nominal light range in nautical miles; 25 m is the charted elevation.
options: A light elevation of 15 metres
A period of 15 minutes
A depth of 15 metres at the light
A nominal range of 15 nautical miles

questions.title: Position-line geometry
questions.prompt: Which pair of intersecting position lines generally has the least favourable fixing geometry?
questions.rationale: Nearly parallel lines magnify the positional effect of small observation errors.
options: Two lines crossing at 95°
Two lines crossing at 90°
Two lines crossing at 85°
Two lines crossing at only 5°

questions.title: Unexpected landfall depth
questions.prompt: An independently checked echo sounding is substantially shallower than the passage plan predicts near landfall. What is the prudent response?
questions.rationale: An unexplained depth discrepancy can indicate a position or datum error and requires immediate assessment.
options: Increase speed so the discrepancy lasts less time
Reduce the planned safety contour to make the alarm stop
Reassess position, tide and clearance immediately and call the Master as required
Assume the seabed must be deeper ahead

questions.title: Routeing guidance use
questions.prompt: Why consult a Mariners’ Routeing Guide during appraisal?
questions.rationale: A routeing guide supplements charts and other current information; it is not a substitute for them.
options: To identify routeing measures, reporting arrangements and navigational considerations for the area
To remove the need for local navigational warnings
To guarantee right of way in every traffic lane
To replace the corrected largest-scale charts

questions.title: Separation zone
questions.prompt: When using an IMO-adopted TSS, what is the normal requirement concerning its separation line or zone?
questions.rationale: Rule 10 requires vessels using a scheme to keep clear of the separating measure so far as practicable.
options: Navigate along it to reduce current effects
Anchor there whenever a lane is busy
Keep clear so far as practicable, subject to the exceptions in Rule 10
Use it as an overtaking lane

questions.title: Set and drift from a fix
questions.prompt: After one hour, the vessel’s observed position is 3 nautical miles east and 4 nautical miles north of its DR position. Assume the difference is entirely due to a steady stream. Calculate set in degrees true and drift in knots, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Stream displacement is 3 east and 4 north in one hour; drift=5 kn and set=atan(3/4)=36.9°T.

questions.title: Counteracting an easterly stream
questions.prompt: A vessel makes 10 kn through the water. Stream sets east at 6 kn. Ignore leeway. Find heading to make a due-north ground track and the speed made good, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: A 6 kn westward water component cancels the stream; north component=sqrt(100−36)=8. Heading=360−asin(.6)=323.1°T.

questions.title: Opposing current passage time
questions.prompt: The heading and intended track are due east. Speed through water is 15 kn and current sets due west at 2 kn. Ignore leeway. How many hours are required for a 65 nautical mile leg?
questions.rationale: Ground speed=15−2=13 kn; time=65/13=5 hours.

questions.title: Leeway direction
questions.prompt: A vessel heads 225°T with 3° leeway to starboard and no current. What is the track through the water?
questions.rationale: Starboard leeway adds 3° clockwise to the heading: 228°T.

questions.title: Compass to true
questions.prompt: Compass heading is 270°. Variation is 8°W and deviation 3°E. What is true heading in whole degrees?
questions.rationale: Signed compass error=−8+3=−5°. True=270−5=265°.

questions.title: Relative bearing
questions.prompt: A vessel’s true heading is 350°. A fixed object is observed at relative bearing 030° clockwise from the bow. What is its true bearing?

questions.title: Chartwork coordinates
questions.prompt: In the training grid, O is the start and P is 8 nautical miles east and 6 nautical miles north of O. Find bearing of P from O and distance OP to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Bearing=atan(8/6)=53.1°T; distance=sqrt(8²+6²)=10 nm.

questions.title: Speed to maintain the plan
questions.prompt: At 0915, the planned waypoint is 27 nautical miles away. It must be reached at 1130. What average speed made good is required?
questions.rationale: Time available=2.25 hours; 27/2.25=12 kn.

questions.title: Mercator distance scale
questions.prompt: When measuring a short distance on a Mercator chart, which latitude scale should normally be used?
questions.rationale: Mercator scale changes with latitude; local latitude scale is used for a nearby distance.
options: The longitude scale regardless of latitude
The latitude scale near the latitude of the measured distance
Only the equatorial latitude scale
The scale from an unrelated chart

questions.title: Crossing the date line along a parallel
questions.prompt: A vessel follows latitude 60°N eastwards from 179°E to 179°W across 180°. Using parallel sailing, find the shorter eastward distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Shorter longitude difference is 2°=120′. Distance=120 cos 60°=60 nm.

questions.title: North-easterly plane sailing
questions.prompt: Using plane sailing, a course of 060°T produces 60 nautical miles of northing. Find distance and departure to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: DLat=D cosC; D=60/.5=120 nm. Departure=120 sin 60°=103.9 nm.

questions.title: Mercator sailing across 180°
questions.prompt: A north-easterly passage runs from longitude 179°E to 175°W by the shorter route. DMP is 480 and DLat is 300′ north. Use tan C=DLo/DMP and D=DLat/cos C. Calculate course and distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Eastward DLo=6°=360′. C=atan(.75)=36.9°; distance=300/.8=375 nm.

questions.title: ETA over a month end
questions.prompt: At 2300 UTC on 31 July, 54 nautical miles remain at a steady 9 kn over ground. What is the ETA?
questions.rationale: 54/9=6 hours; six hours after 2300 on 31 July is 0500 on 1 August.
options: 0400 UTC on 1 August
0600 UTC on 1 August
0500 UTC on 1 August
0500 UTC on 31 July

questions.title: Unfit relieving officer
questions.prompt: The relieving officer appears too fatigued to keep a safe watch. What should the outgoing OOW do?
questions.rationale: The watch must not be handed to a person apparently incapable of carrying it out effectively.
options: Leave the bridge and record the concern later
Let the lookout take charge of navigation
Retain the watch and inform the Master rather than hand over to an unfit officer
Hand over because the watch period has ended

questions.title: Sole lookout conditions
questions.prompt: For an OOW acting as sole lookout in daylight, which conditions are relevant? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Daylight sole lookout is conditional on an assessment and immediate availability of assistance.
options: Daylight makes a separate risk assessment unnecessary
A careful assessment establishes that it is safe
Relevant traffic, weather, visibility and bridge workload are considered
Assistance can be summoned immediately

questions.title: Gyro error from corrected amplitude
questions.prompt: An amplitude observation has been fully corrected to a true bearing of 268°. The simultaneous gyro bearing is 270°. What is gyro error?
questions.rationale: True−gyro=−2°, meaning 2°W.
options: No error

questions.title: Total power failure
questions.prompt: The bridge loses main electrical power at night. Which actions are appropriate parts of the immediate response? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The bridge must establish the ship’s actual condition and coordinate the blackout response.
options: Maintain lookout and assess nearby traffic and hazards
Establish which steering and navigation services remain available
Call the Master and communicate with the engine room
Assume the vessel will keep its original track indefinitely

questions.title: Steering check meaning
questions.prompt: What makes a steering operational check meaningful?
questions.rationale: A functional check verifies response and relevant arrangements, not merely control movement.
options: Confirming actual rudder response and required control and communication arrangements
Watching only the wheel move without checking rudder response
Checking only that the steering switch is labelled
Assuming the previous voyage test remains sufficient

questions.title: Radar limitations near ice
questions.prompt: Which statement about radar detection of ice is correct?
questions.rationale: Low profile, sea state and reflectivity can limit radar detection; absence of an echo is not proof of no ice.
options: Rain clutter elimination guarantees ice detection
Every iceberg gives a strong echo at the same range
AIS identifies all floating ice
Small or low ice may be difficult to detect, so radar must be supported by other information and lookout

questions.title: Using ice reports
questions.prompt: A ship receives a recent ice-edge report. How should it be used?
questions.rationale: Ice moves and information ages; report timing and corroborating observations matter.
options: As evidence that the area outside the reported line is always ice-free
As an exact stationary boundary for the rest of the voyage
As permission to dispense with the lookout
Together with its observation time, expected ice movement, current reports and actual conditions

questions.title: Reference levels and heights
questions.prompt: Match each abbreviation or term to its meaning.
questions.rationale: Tidal reference levels and vessel heights use different origins and must not be interchanged.
definitions: Highest astronomical tide under average meteorological conditions
Lowest astronomical tide under average meteorological conditions
Height above chart datum of a feature that dries
Height from current waterline to the vessel’s highest relevant point

questions.title: Tidal range
questions.prompt: Predicted high water is 5.4 m and the associated low water is 1.2 m, on the same datum. Find the tidal range.

questions.title: Allowing for squat
questions.prompt: The actual water depth is 9.1 m and the ship’s static draught is 8.1 m. Squat adds 0.4 m to draught. Ignore all other effects. Calculate the resulting under-keel clearance.

questions.title: Falling-tide interpolation
questions.prompt: Use the supplied falling-tide training curve. High water is 0930 at 6.0 m; low water is 1530 at 2.0 m. Read the curve by straight-line interpolation between its plotted points. What is the height at 1200?
questions.rationale: At 2.5 hours after HW, fall fraction interpolates from .25 at hour 2 to .50 at hour 3: .375. Height=6−4×.375=4.5 m.

questions.title: Latest tide-window time
questions.prompt: Use the falling-tide training curve. High water is 0930 at 6.0 m; low water is 1530 at 2.0 m. During this falling tide, when does the height reach the required minimum of 2.8 m?
questions.rationale: Fall fraction=(6−2.8)/4=.8, reached four hours after HW at 1330.

questions.title: Prediction and observed level
questions.prompt: Actual sea level at a port is lower than the prediction during unusual weather. What should the OOW do?
questions.rationale: Predictions describe astronomical tides; meteorological effects and observations must inform clearance assessments.
options: Use reliable observed information and reassess the planned depth margins
Ignore the discrepancy if the tide table is current
Add the discrepancy to draught with the wrong sign automatically
Treat the prediction as an exact guarantee

questions.title: Extent of a passage plan
questions.prompt: What is the intended extent of an appropriate voyage passage plan?
questions.rationale: Appraisal and planning cover the whole intended voyage, including departures and approaches.
options: Only waypoints that are visible on radar
Only the departure manoeuvre
The complete voyage from berth to berth, including pilotage legs
Only the open-sea part outside pilotage waters

questions.title: Under-keel appraisal
questions.prompt: Which matters can affect the depth margin used in passage appraisal? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Clearance appraisal considers dynamic vessel effects and uncertainty as well as static draught.
options: The assumption that static draught is the only relevant factor
Tide and uncertainty in actual water level
Accuracy of charted depth and position
Squat and vessel motion

questions.title: Weather-driven alteration
questions.prompt: Conditions make a planned exposed leg unsuitable. Which response best follows passage-planning principles?
questions.rationale: A plan is reassessed when the underlying conditions change.
options: Reappraise alternatives, amend the plan with the Master and brief those implementing it
Continue because the original route was approved
Choose an unassessed shortcut on the plotter
Delete the old route so no record of the decision remains

questions.title: Chart information currency
questions.prompt: Which is the appropriate preparation for a chart needed on passage?
questions.rationale: Edition status, corrections and current warnings together affect chart reliability.
options: Assume the chart is current because it was purchased recently
Check the appropriate edition and apply relevant current corrections and warnings
Rely on an old plotted track instead of checking chart information
Apply only corrections to the destination harbour

questions.title: A buoy as the only reference
questions.prompt: Why is an isolated buoy generally weaker than a fixed shore object as the sole reference for a position fix?
questions.rationale: A floating aid can be off station; independent checks are needed.
options: Its charted position changes every second by definition
It can be displaced from its charted position
It cannot have a radar reflector
Its colour is always invisible in daylight

questions.title: A missing expected light
questions.prompt: A charted light is not seen at landfall. What is the appropriate interpretation?
questions.rationale: Failure to see an expected aid is not a unique position solution and does not remove the danger.
options: The coast must be clear if no light is seen
The danger marked by the light has disappeared
The vessel must be outside the light’s nominal range
The absence needs investigation; position, visibility, range and light status may all be relevant

questions.title: Radar near turbines
questions.prompt: Which passage-planning precaution is appropriate where wind turbines may affect radar observations?
questions.rationale: Equipment limitations should be anticipated and cross-checks planned.
options: Treat every echo in the wind farm as a ship
Allow for possible clutter or false echoes and plan suitable independent checks
Use turbine echoes as the only position reference
Switch radar off throughout the passage

questions.title: Other COLREG duties in a TSS
questions.prompt: A vessel is proceeding correctly in its TSS lane. What does Rule 10 imply about its other COLREG obligations?
questions.rationale: Rule 10(a) expressly does not relieve a vessel of obligations under other rules.
options: The lane user can maintain speed regardless of collision risk
Lookout obligations cease inside the lane
All ships crossing must keep clear regardless of other rules
They still apply; compliance with Rule 10 gives no general exemption

questions.title: Different TSS manoeuvres
questions.prompt: Match each manoeuvre with the normal Rule 10 approach.
questions.rationale: Crossing, joining and lane-following have different requirements.
definitions: Heading as nearly at right angles to traffic flow as practicable
Join at as small an angle to traffic flow as practicable
Follow the general direction of flow in the appropriate lane

questions.title: Westerly heading with southerly stream
questions.prompt: A vessel heads 270°T at 12 kn through the water; stream sets 180°T at 5 kn. Ignore leeway. Find true course and speed over ground to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Ground vector is 12 west and 5 south: COG=270−atan(5/12)=247.4°; SOG=13 kn.

questions.title: Making good east
questions.prompt: With 10 kn through the water and a stream setting due north at 6 kn, find the heading required to make good due east and the speed made good. Ignore leeway; give one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Water vector must be 8 east and 6 south; heading=126.9°T, ground speed=8 kn.

questions.title: Port leeway
questions.prompt: Heading is 045°T and leeway is 4° to port. With no current, what is track through the water?
questions.rationale: Port leeway is anticlockwise from heading:45−4=41°T.

questions.title: Compass course across north
questions.prompt: Required true heading is 358°. Variation is 2°W and deviation 5°W. Calculate compass heading in whole degrees, in the range 000° to 359°.
questions.rationale: Total error=7°W; compass=358+7=365°, reduced to 005°.

questions.title: Gyro error across north
questions.prompt: A transit bears 002°T and simultaneously reads 355°G. What is gyro error?
questions.rationale: 002°T is equivalent to 362°; 362−355=+7°, or 7°E.

questions.title: Maintaining true course
questions.prompt: Gyro error changes from 3°E to 1°E. What change to the gyro-course order maintains the same true heading?
questions.rationale: Gyro=true−east error. A reduction of east error by 2° requires gyro order to increase 2°.
options: No change is required
Increase the gyro-course order by 4°
Decrease the gyro-course order by 2°
Increase the gyro-course order by 2°

questions.title: Observation timing
questions.prompt: Why should ranges or bearings used for a fix be taken as nearly simultaneously as practicable?
questions.rationale: Time separation causes lines to refer to different vessel positions unless properly advanced.
options: All instruments become inaccurate after one second
Simultaneous observations remove all chart error
The vessel moves between observations, potentially displacing the position lines
Shore objects move at the vessel’s speed

questions.title: Running-fix uncertainty
questions.prompt: Which factor particularly affects a running fix compared with a simultaneous fix?
questions.rationale: A running fix adds an estimated advancement between observations, introducing motion uncertainty.
options: The colour of the plotting pencil alone
Uncertainty in the vessel’s ground movement between the observations
The shore object being fixed to land
The fact that bearings use angular units

questions.title: Westward parallel passage
questions.prompt: A ship follows latitude 30°N westwards through 1° of longitude. Using parallel sailing, find distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: D=60 cos 30°=51.96 nm, rounded 52.0 nm.

questions.title: South-westerly plane sailing
questions.prompt: A short plane-sailing leg has 30 nautical miles southing and 40 nautical miles westward departure. Calculate true course and distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: South-west quadrant:course=180+atan(40/30)=233.1°T; distance=50 nm.

questions.title: South-easterly Mercator passage
questions.prompt: For a south-easterly rhumb line, DLo is 180′ east, DMP is 240 and DLat is 192′ south. Use tan(quadrantal course)=DLo/DMP. Find true course and distance to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Quadrantal course=36.87° east of south; true course 143.1°.Distance=192/.8=240 nm.

questions.title: Rhumb-line property
questions.prompt: Which property distinguishes a rhumb line on a Mercator chart?
questions.rationale: A rhumb line has constant true direction; a great circle is the shortest spherical route and normally changes direction.
options: It crosses meridians at a constant angle and is plotted as a straight line
It is always shorter than the great-circle route
It can exist only along the equator
It crosses every parallel at a different heading

questions.title: Half-hour time zone
questions.prompt: Departure is 0330 on 12 June at UTC+5 hours 30 minutes. Passage duration is 12 hours. Arrival port is UTC−3. What is local ETA?
questions.rationale: Departure=2200 UTC 11 June; arrival=1000 UTC 12 June; UTC−3 gives 0700 on 12 June.
options: 2200 on 11 June
1800 on 12 June
0700 on 13 June
0700 on 12 June

questions.title: Developing restricted visibility
questions.prompt: Visibility deteriorates unexpectedly. Which bridge actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Restricted visibility requires prompt assessment, the appropriate bridge team and applicable procedures.
options: Reassess safe speed and collision risk
Call the Master under standing orders
Ensure an effective lookout and apply the required restricted-visibility procedures
Wait for a close-quarters situation before acting

questions.title: Closed-loop communication
questions.prompt: Which exchange best illustrates closed-loop communication of an engine order?
questions.rationale: Repeat-back and verification reduce misunderstanding during routine and emergency communications.
options: The sender assumes an unheard order was accepted
A third person records the order after the watch ends
The receiver says nothing and changes an unrelated control
The receiver repeats the order and the sender checks that the repeat is correct

questions.title: Compass check using Polaris
questions.prompt: A Polaris observation has already been corrected to true bearing 359.2°. Gyro bearing is 001.2°. What is gyro error?
questions.rationale: Treat 359.2° as−0.8° near north; true−gyro=−2.0°.
options: No error

questions.title: Correcting a bridge record
questions.prompt: A bridge-log entry contains an error. What is the appropriate general approach?
questions.rationale: Records should retain an auditable history of corrections, with the appropriate attribution and timing.
options: Rewrite the entire page without a correction record
Make a traceable correction under the ship’s recordkeeping procedure
Leave an identified material error uncorrected
Erase the original entry so the alteration cannot be seen

questions.title: Relief during a manoeuvre
questions.prompt: An alteration to avoid traffic is in progress at watch-change time. What is the normal handover approach unless the Master directs otherwise?
questions.rationale: A manoeuvre or other avoidance action should normally be completed before the watch is handed over.
options: Complete the action and establish a clear situation before transferring the watch
Transfer immediately regardless of the developing manoeuvre
Leave the bridge as soon as the scheduled time arrives
Let the incoming OOW infer the alteration without a briefing

questions.title: Interpreting a sign of ice
questions.prompt: A pale glow is observed under low cloud toward the horizon in an ice region. What does this indicate?
questions.rationale: An optical indication suggests possible nearby ice but does not establish its precise location or extent.
options: A guaranteed ice-free channel
Possible ice blink requiring corroboration and caution
The exact range of an iceberg
Proof that radar settings are correct

questions.title: Upper-deck ice accretion
questions.prompt: Why is accumulating ice on upper decks a concern for the bridge team?
questions.rationale: Ice high in the vessel raises weight and potentially KG while also creating operational hazards.
options: It guarantees more freeboard
It removes the need to assess wind effects
It adds high weight and can adversely affect stability as well as safe deck access
It always lowers the centre of gravity

questions.title: Astronomical range and actual tide
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes spring-tide prediction from actual observed water level?
questions.rationale: Sun–Moon alignment affects astronomical range; meteorological effects remain possible.
options: Weather has no effect during a spring tide
The word spring refers only to the season
Spring tides guarantee the largest observed water level on every occasion
Spring tides generally have larger astronomical range, but weather can still modify the observed level

questions.title: Maximum tide for an overhead passage
questions.prompt: A bridge has charted clearance 26.0 m above HAT. HAT is 4.0 m above datum. Air draught is 27.0 m and required overhead margin is 1.0 m. Ignoring other effects, what is the greatest tide height permitting this margin?
questions.rationale: Bridge underside is 30 m above datum; 30−tide−27>=1, so tide<=2.0 m.

questions.title: Air-draught origin
questions.prompt: For an overhead-clearance calculation, air draught is measured from:
questions.rationale: Air draught is the above-water height of the vessel; it is not keel-to-mast height.
options: The keel to the top of the mast
The sea bed to the masthead
The vessel’s current waterline to its highest relevant point
Chart datum to the bridge underside

questions.title: Tide over midnight
questions.prompt: Use the supplied rising-tide training curve. Low water is 2330 on 12 September at 0.8 m; high water is 0530 on 13 September at 4.8 m. Find height at 0130 on 13 September, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: 0130 is 2 hours after LW; fraction=.20.Height=.8+4×.20=1.6 m.

questions.title: Required height after midnight
questions.prompt: Use the supplied rising-tide training curve. Low water is 2330 at 0.8 m; high water six hours later is 4.8 m. At what time next day does the rising tide first reach 4.0 m?
questions.rationale: Fraction=(4−.8)/4=.80; four hours after 2330 is 0330 next day.

questions.title: A drying depth from sounding
questions.prompt: A corrected sounding shows 0.9 m of water above a feature when tide height is 1.5 m above chart datum. Find the feature’s drying height, to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: Reduced depth=.9−1.5=−.6 m, meaning a drying height of.6 m above datum.

questions.title: Density and mass
questions.prompt: A liquid cargo occupies 800 m³ and has density 0.90 t/m³. Calculate its mass in tonnes.
questions.rationale: Mass=density×volume=.90×800=720 t.

questions.title: Hydrostatic interpolation
questions.prompt: Training hydrostatic data at the stated water density give displacement 8,000 t at 6.0 m mean draught and 10,000 t at 7.0 m. Assume linear interpolation over this interval. Find displacement at 6.4 m.

questions.title: TPC at dock-water density
questions.prompt: TPC is 18.0 t/cm in seawater of density 1.025 t/m³. At the same waterplane area, calculate TPC in dock water of density 1.010 t/m³, to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: TPC scales with density at constant waterplane area:18×1.010/1.025=17.74 t/cm.

questions.title: Weight for a small immersion
questions.prompt: TPC remains constant at 20 t/cm during loading. What weight can be loaded to increase draught by 12 cm?
questions.rationale: Weight=TPC×centimetres=20×12=240 t.

questions.title: Calculating fresh water allowance
questions.prompt: At the relevant displacement of 10,000 t, salt-water TPC is 25 t/cm. Use FWA(mm)=displacement/(4×TPC). Calculate FWA.

questions.title: Calculating dock water allowance
questions.prompt: FWA is 180 mm. Dock-water density is 1.015 t/m³ and seawater density 1.025 t/m³. Use DWA=FWA×(1.025−dock density)/.025. Calculate DWA.

questions.title: Block coefficient from dimensions
questions.prompt: Underwater volume is 16,800 m³, length between perpendiculars 150 m, moulded breadth 20 m and draught 8 m. Calculate block coefficient to two decimal places.

questions.title: Loading with dock-water allowance
questions.prompt: Summer salt-water draught is 8.00 m. DWA is 0.12 m. Present draught in dock water is 7.80 m and dock-water TPC stays 18 t/cm. Ignoring voyage consumption and trim, calculate maximum additional cargo to the corresponding dock-water load limit.
questions.rationale: Permitted dock-water draught=8+.12=8.12 m; increase=.32 m=32 cm; cargo=32×18=576 t.

questions.title: Initial equilibrium conditions
questions.prompt: Match the initial transverse condition to its metacentric relationship.
questions.rationale: Initial stability depends on the signed separation of M and G.
definitions: M below G: negative GM
M above G: positive GM
M and G coincide: zero GM

questions.title: Effective GM
questions.prompt: KM is 8.30 m and KG 6.80 m. Free-surface correction is 0.15 m. Calculate effective GM to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Effective GM=KM−KG−FSC=8.30−6.80−.15=1.35 m.

questions.title: Righting moment
questions.prompt: Displacement is 7,500 t and GZ at the specified heel angle is 0.42 m. Calculate moment of statical stability in tonne-metres.
questions.rationale: Moment=displacement×GZ=7500×.42=3150 tonne-metres.

questions.title: A vertical shift within the ship
questions.prompt: On an 8,000 t vessel, 100 t is moved vertically from 2.0 m to 10.0 m above keel. Displacement is unchanged. Calculate the rise of the ship’s G.
questions.rationale: GG=weight×vertical distance/displacement=100×8/8000=.10 m.

questions.title: KG after loading high cargo
questions.prompt: Initial displacement is 6,000 t at KG 5.00 m. Load 800 t at KG 12.00 m. Ignoring free-surface effects, calculate final KG to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Final vertical moment=30000+9600=39600 tm; final displacement 6800 t; KG=5.8235 m, rounded 5.82 m.

questions.title: KG after discharging high cargo
questions.prompt: A vessel displaces 10,000 t at KG 6.00 m. Discharge 400 t from KG 10.00 m. Calculate final KG to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Remaining moment=60000−4000=56000 tm; displacement 9600 t; KG=5.8333 m, rounded 5.83 m.

questions.title: Suspending an onboard weight
questions.prompt: A 100 t onboard weight is lifted clear of its support at KG 2.0 m and hangs freely from a crane suspension point 14.0 m above keel. Vessel displacement remains 6,000 t. Find the virtual rise of the ship’s G.
questions.rationale: Once freely suspended, the load acts at its point of suspension. Rise=100×(14−2)/6000=.20 m.

questions.title: List from a transverse shift
questions.prompt: A vessel of displacement 12,000 t has effective GM 1.00 m. A 200 t weight shifts 6.0 m transversely from the centreline. Assume small-angle theory and unchanged GM. Calculate the resulting angle of list to one decimal place.
questions.rationale: tan(list)=w×d/(displacement×GM)=1200/12000=.1; list=5.7°.

questions.title: Longitudinal tank division
questions.prompt: A rectangular slack tank is divided by an effective centreline longitudinal bulkhead into two equal, unconnected slack tanks. At equal liquid density and length, the total free-surface moment becomes what fraction of the undivided value?
questions.rationale: FSM is proportional to length×breadth³. Two tanks of half breadth give 2×(1/2)³=1/4 of the original moment.
options: One half
Twice
One quarter
The same

questions.title: Reading a stability curve
questions.prompt: Use the training GZ curve. Read the angle of maximum GZ and the angle where positive stability ends. Give whole degrees.
questions.rationale: The plotted maximum is at 35° and the positive curve returns to zero at 70°.

questions.title: Arithmetic mean draught
questions.prompt: Forward draught is 4.20 m and aft draught 5.00 m. Calculate arithmetic mean draught.

questions.title: True mean draught at LCF
questions.prompt: Forward draught is 4.50 m and aft draught 5.50 m over 100 m LBP. LCF lies 10 m aft of amidships. Assume a straight waterline and take true mean draught as draught at LCF. Calculate it to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: LCF is 60 m aft of FP; draught there=4.50+(60/100)×1.00=5.10 m.

questions.title: A trimming moment
questions.prompt: A 250 t weight shifts 20 m longitudinally. Calculate the magnitude of its trimming moment.
questions.rationale: Moment=250×20=5000 tonne-metres.

questions.title: Change of trim from moment
questions.prompt: A trimming moment of 5,000 tonne-metres acts on a vessel with constant MCTC 200 tonne-metres per centimetre. Calculate change of trim in centimetres.
questions.rationale: Change of trim=5000/200=25 cm.

questions.title: Correcting stern trim
questions.prompt: A vessel is trimmed 0.40 m by the stern. MCTC stays 150 tonne-metres/cm. What weight must be moved 60 m forward to remove the trim, with displacement unchanged?
questions.rationale: Moment needed=40×150=6000 tm; weight=6000/60=100 t, moved forward.

questions.title: Draughts after an off-centre load
questions.prompt: A vessel is initially on even keel at 5.00 m. LBP 120 m; LCF amidships; TPC 20 t/cm; MCTC 180 tonne-metres/cm, all constant. Load 240 t at 30 m aft of LCF. Find final forward and aft draughts to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Parallel sinkage=240/20=12 cm. Stern trim=240×30/180=40 cm, split 20 cm at each end. F=5+.12−.20=4.92; A=5+.12+.20=5.32.

questions.title: Changing an existing trim
questions.prompt: Forward draught is 5.00 m and aft draught 5.40 m. LCF is amidships and MCTC stays 200 tonne-metres/cm. Shift 200 t from 20 m aft of LCF to 20 m forward. Find final draughts to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Forward moment=200×40=8000 tm; trim change 40 cm by head. Each end changes 20 cm; F 5.20, A 5.20. No parallel change for an onboard shift.

questions.title: Enclosed-space casualty
questions.prompt: A person collapses inside an enclosed space. Which immediate actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: A spontaneous unprotected rescue can create further casualties; summon and prepare an organised response.
options: Follow the ship’s enclosed-space rescue procedure
Prevent an unplanned, unprotected entry
Enter immediately without equipment because the casualty is visible
Raise the alarm and summon the trained rescue response

questions.title: Mooring-line hazard
questions.prompt: A mooring line is heavily loaded during a rising tide. What should the deck watch do?
questions.rationale: Tensioned lines and changing leads are hazardous; adjustment must be controlled and people kept clear.
options: Step across the tensioned line to inspect it
Stand in a bight so the line can be eased quickly
Keep people clear of hazardous line paths and arrange controlled adjustment under the ship’s procedures
Release all lines simultaneously without coordination

questions.title: Hot-work permit
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a hot-work permit system?
questions.rationale: A permit provides controlled authorisation with defined conditions; it does not eliminate changing hazards.
options: To verify assessed hazards, isolations, precautions and authorisation before the work proceeds
To permit welding in any tank without testing
To replace the risk assessment completely
To remove the need for fire precautions once signed

questions.title: Integrity and closures
questions.prompt: Match each description to its meaning.
questions.rationale: Watertight and weathertight are different performance requirements; correct closures must be maintained.
definitions: Check and secure the required closures before exposure increases
Prevents passage of water in either direction under the designed head
Prevents water entering the ship in any sea condition

questions.title: Bunkering preparation
questions.prompt: Which checks are appropriate before starting fuel transfer? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Transfer must begin only after receiving capacity, communication and spill controls have been checked.
options: Arrange spill-prevention and containment measures
Confirm receiving tanks, available capacity and valve alignment
Agree communication and the emergency stop procedure
Begin at maximum rate before confirming the receiving tank

questions.title: Garbage annex
questions.prompt: Which MARPOL Annex deals with pollution by garbage?
questions.rationale: Annex V concerns garbage; Annex I oil, II noxious liquid substances in bulk andIV sewage.
options: Annex IV
Annex V
Annex II
Annex I

questions.title: Packaged dangerous goods
questions.prompt: Before handling packaged dangerous goods, which information or controls should be checked? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Cargo identification, approved stowage/segregation and emergency information guide safe handling.
options: Cargo identity, markings and relevant dangerous-goods documentation
Applicable emergency information and protective measures
Identify an unknown substance by smelling it closely
Stowage, segregation and securing requirements

questions.title: Purpose of the safety management system
questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a safety management system under the ISM Code?
questions.rationale: The ISM framework organises responsibilities and safeguards for safety and environmental protection.
options: A commercial schedule that replaces the Master’s judgement
A document that removes the need for drills
A structured system for safe ship operations and pollution prevention with defined responsibilities and procedures
An optional list used only after an accident

questions.title: Normal minimum rest
questions.prompt: For an adult seafarer subject to the UK normal minimum-rest rules, with no authorised exception or emergency, which minimum pair applies?
questions.rationale: The normal UK regime requires at least 10 hours rest in any 24 hours and 77 in any 7 days.
options: 10 hours in any 24 hours and 77 hours in any 7 days
12 hours in any 24 hours and 60 hours in any 7 days
8 hours in any 24 hours and 56 hours in any 7 days
6 hours in any 24 hours and 72 hours in any 7 days

questions.title: M-notice functions
questions.prompt: Match each notice series to its general function.
questions.rationale: The notice series have different functions; the legal effect depends on the notice and enabling legislation.
definitions: Conveys mandatory requirements where specified under legislation
Gives marine safety or related guidance
Gives information commonly limited to a particular time or audience

questions.title: Law of flotation
questions.prompt: For a freely floating vessel in equilibrium, which statement is correct?
questions.rationale: Buoyancy balances the vessel’s weight in floating equilibrium.
options: The vessel’s weight equals the weight of the water it displaces
The ship must have neutral transverse stability
The water displaced has zero weight
The vessel’s volume always equals its mass numerically

questions.title: Waterplane coefficient
questions.prompt: Waterplane area is 1,800 m². Length is 100 m and breadth 24 m for this coefficient calculation. Find waterplane coefficient to two decimal places.

questions.title: Displacement volume
questions.prompt: A vessel displaces 8,200 t in seawater of density 1.025 t/m³. Calculate displaced volume in cubic metres.
questions.rationale: Volume=mass/density=8200/1.025=8000 m³.

questions.title: Large draught change
questions.prompt: At the relevant density, training hydrostatic data give 6,000 t at 5.0 m, 8,000 t at 6.0 m and 10,400 t at 7.0 m. Interpolate linearly within each interval. From 5.0 m initially, what cargo mass raises mean draught to 6.5 m? Ignore other weight changes.
questions.rationale: Final displacement=8000+.5×2400=9200 t; cargo=9200−6000=3200 t. Use displacement data across the large draught change.

questions.title: Moving to less-dense water
questions.prompt: A vessel moves into less-dense water without changing weight. What must happen to displaced volume?
questions.rationale: At fixed mass, displaced volume=mass/density, so reducing density increases volume.
options: It increases so the weight of displaced water still equals the vessel’s weight
It becomes equal to deadweight
It decreases because the ship has lost mass
It stays fixed regardless of density

questions.title: Fresh-water immersion allowance
questions.prompt: Displacement is 14,400 t and salt-water TPC 30 t/cm. Use FWA(mm)=displacement/(4×TPC). Calculate FWA.

questions.title: Freeboard after discharge
questions.prompt: With constant TPC 30 t/cm, 600 t of cargo is discharged. Ignore trim. By how many metres does freeboard increase?
questions.rationale: Draught decreases 600/30=20 cm; freeboard increases.20 m.

questions.title: Selecting a load-line limit
questions.prompt: Which checks are relevant when deciding the permitted loading limit for a voyage? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: The permissible loading condition depends on assigned marks, the voyage area/season and water-density allowances.
options: Water density and the relevant fresh/dock-water allowance
Applicable load-line zones and seasonal periods
The appropriate assigned load-line marks
Use the deepest mark regardless of zone and season

questions.title: Neutral initial stability
questions.prompt: Under ideal initial-stability theory, what condition corresponds to neutral initial stability?
questions.rationale: When G and M coincide, initial GM is zero and the initial restoring tendency vanishes.
options: G is necessarily below the keel
Displacement is zero
GM is zero
GM is always strongly positive

questions.title: Small-angle righting lever
questions.prompt: Effective GM is 1.80 m. Use GZ=GM×sin(heel) at the given small angle of 10°. Calculate GZ to three decimal places.

questions.title: Different GZ curve
questions.prompt: Use the training curve. Read maximum GZ to one decimal place and the angle of vanishing stability in whole degrees.
questions.rationale: The plotted maximum GZ is.9 m at 40° and the positive range ends at 80°.

questions.title: Combined free-surface moments
questions.prompt: At displacement 10,000 t, two slack tanks have free-surface moments 600 and 900 tonne-metres. Calculate the total virtual rise of G to two decimal places.

questions.title: Removing an off-centre G
questions.prompt: A vessel displaces 10,000 t and G is 0.12 m to starboard of the centreline. What distance must a 200 t onboard weight move to port to bring G to the centreline? Ignore all other changes.
questions.rationale: Moment required=10000×.12=1200 tm; distance=1200/200=6.0 m to port.

questions.title: List after an off-centre load
questions.prompt: After loading, final displacement is 6,000 t and effective GM 0.90 m. The only transverse heeling moment is from a 100 t load placed 6.0 m to starboard of the centreline. Using tan(list)=heeling moment/(displacement×GM), calculate list to one decimal place.

questions.title: Directions of movement of G
questions.prompt: Ignoring free surface, match each operation to the direction in which G moves.
questions.rationale: Adding weight moves G towards it; removing weight moves G away; an onboard transfer moves G parallel to the transfer.
terms: Load a weight above the existing G
Discharge a weight above the existing G
Shift an onboard weight to port
definitions: Towards port parallel to the shift
Downwards away from the removed weight
Upwards towards the added weight

questions.title: A freely suspended load
questions.prompt: For stability assessment after a ship’s crane has lifted a load clear, where is that freely suspended load treated as acting?
questions.rationale: The effective action is at the suspension point, not at the hanging load’s own centre.
options: At its point of suspension
At the sea surface regardless of crane geometry
At its original stowage position
At the keel directly below the hook

questions.title: Suspected angle of loll
questions.prompt: A vessel with suspected negative initial GM heels without an established off-centre weight. What is the appropriate principle for deciding a correction?
questions.rationale: Loll is associated with negative GM; an unassessed transverse shift can be dangerous. Use the approved stability information to address the underlying condition.
options: Treat the heel as proof of a large positive GM
Assume it is an ordinary list and shift a large weight across immediately
Have the Master assess the stability condition and restore positive stability using the approved information
Ignore free-surface effects because the vessel is heeled

questions.title: Density and free surface
questions.prompt: For the same slack-tank geometry and free-surface shape, what happens to its free-surface moment if liquid density doubles?
questions.rationale: Free-surface moment is proportional to liquid density for fixed free-surface geometry.
options: It doubles
It is unchanged
It halves
It falls to zero

questions.title: Longitudinal centres
questions.prompt: Match each abbreviation to its definition.
questions.rationale: LCF concerns waterplane area, LCG mass and LCB displaced volume.
definitions: Longitudinal centroid of the waterplane area
Longitudinal position of the centre of the displaced volume
Longitudinal position of the vessel’s centre of gravity

questions.title: Direction of trim
questions.prompt: Forward draught is 6.00 m and aft draught 5.40 m. What is the trim?
questions.rationale: Forward draught exceeds aft by.60 m, so trim is.60 m by the head.
options: 0.60 m by the head
0.60 m by the stern
No trim
5.70 m by the head

questions.title: MCTC application
questions.prompt: Constant MCTC is 125 tonne-metres/cm. A 2,500 tonne-metre trimming moment is applied. Find magnitude of change of trim in centimetres.

questions.title: Longitudinal transfer distance
questions.prompt: A 150 t weight moves from 10 m forward of LCF to 30 m aft of LCF. MCTC stays 200 tonne-metres/cm. Find the sternward change of trim in centimetres.
questions.rationale: Transfer distance=10+30=40 m; moment=6000 tm; trim change=6000/200=30 cm by stern.

questions.title: Forward LCF and mean draught
questions.prompt: Forward draught 4.80 m; aft 5.40 m; LBP 120 m; LCF 12 m forward of amidships. Assume a straight waterline and true mean draught equal to draught at LCF. Calculate TMD to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: LCF is 48 m aft of FP. Draught at LCF=4.8+(.6×48/120)=5.04 m.

questions.title: Loading at LCF
questions.prompt: A vessel is initially on even keel at 6.00 m. Load 300 t exactly at LCF; TPC stays 25 t/cm. Ignore changes in hydrostatic characteristics. Find final forward and aft draughts to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: No trimming moment at LCF; parallel sinkage=300/25=12 cm. Both draughts become 6.12 m.

questions.title: Discharge aft of LCF
questions.prompt: A vessel is initially on even keel at 6.00 m. LCF is amidships; LBP 100 m; TPC 20 t/cm; MCTC 150 tonne-metres/cm, all constant. Discharge 200 t from 30 m aft of LCF. Find final forward and aft draughts to two decimal places.
questions.rationale: Parallel rise=200/20=10 cm. Trim change=200×30/150=40 cm by head, split 20 cm each end. F=6−.10+.20=6.10; A=6−.10−.20=5.70 m.

questions.title: Gangway as draught changes
questions.prompt: During discharge alongside, a gangway becomes excessively steep. What should the deck watch do?
questions.rationale: Access arrangements need continuing monitoring as draught, tide and ship position change.
options: Leave the problem to visitors to manage
Remove lighting to discourage use
Arrange a safe adjustment or alternative access and keep the access route properly controlled
Allow access to continue because the gangway was safe at arrival

questions.title: Stress during cargo operations
questions.prompt: Which practices help control hull stress during cargo and ballast operations? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Intermediate conditions can exceed structural limits even when the final condition is acceptable.
options: Check only the final displacement and ignore the loading sequence
Monitor actual cargo and ballast distribution
Follow the approved loading sequence and relevant limits
Check intermediate as well as final loading conditions

questions.title: Fire during a port watch
questions.prompt: A fire is discovered near cargo operations. What is an appropriate immediate response?
questions.rationale: Alarm and a coordinated response are essential; affected operations must be controlled safely.
options: Keep the incident unreported to avoid delay
Continue cargo operations until smoke reaches the bridge
Enter the area alone without raising the alarm
Raise the alarm and initiate the ship’s emergency response, including safe suspension of affected operations

questions.title: Unexpected ballast transfer
questions.prompt: An unplanned ballast transfer is observed during cargo operations. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Ballast changes affect draught, stability, trim and stress and must remain coordinated with the plan.
options: Establish what transfer is occurring and coordinate its safe control
Check the loading plan, stability and stress implications
Notify the responsible personnel and record the relevant changes
Assume any transfer is harmless if the ship remains upright

questions.title: Plastic waste at sea
questions.prompt: During normal operations, with no applicable Annex V exception, which statement about disposal of plastic garbage into the sea is correct?
questions.rationale: Annex V prohibits routine discharge of plastics into the sea. Regulation 7 contains exceptional safety and accidental-loss provisions; these are excluded by the question.
options: It is permitted if the plastic is chopped up
It is permitted after 12 nautical miles in all cases
It is prohibited, including beyond the normal distance limits used for some other garbage
It is required when reception facilities are inconvenient

questions.title: Sewage annex
questions.prompt: Which MARPOL Annex principally addresses pollution by sewage from ships?
questions.rationale: Annex IV addresses sewage; I oil, III harmful substances in packaged form andVI air pollution.
options: Annex III
Annex I
Annex VI
Annex IV

questions.title: Fuel routed to the wrong tank
questions.prompt: Fuel transfer is found to be entering an unintended tank. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: A misrouting must be brought under control before overflow; communication and verified alignment are essential.
options: Change valves blindly while maintaining full transfer rate
Assess and respond to any overflow or pollution risk
Stop or safely suspend transfer and communicate with the supplying station
Confirm tank levels and the valve arrangement before any restart

questions.title: Master’s safety authority
questions.prompt: Commercial instructions would conflict with the Master’s decision needed for safety and pollution prevention. How should the safety-management arrangements treat the Master’s authority?
questions.rationale: The ISM framework requires the SMS to address the Master’s overriding authority regarding safety and pollution prevention.
options: Allow the charterer to cancel safety procedures verbally
Make the commercial schedule automatically take precedence
Recognise the Master’s overriding authority and responsibility for those decisions
Require the bridge to continue regardless of navigational danger

questions.title: Onboard complaints
questions.prompt: Which principle belongs in an MLC-compliant onboard complaint procedure?
questions.rationale: MLC complaint arrangements protect the right to complain and should safeguard against victimisation.
options: Seafarers can raise complaints through the procedure without victimisation
All complaints must remain undisclosed to the seafarer who made them
Complaints may be punished merely for being made
The procedure must forbid access to external competent authorities

questions.title: Daily rest pattern
questions.prompt: Assume an adult seafarer is subject to the normal UK rest rules, with no exception or emergency, and that weekly totals and intervals between rest periods comply. Which pattern meets both the 10-hour daily minimum and the normal split-rest rule?
questions.rationale: Normal rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours. Total 6+4=10; 5+5 lacks a 6-hour period; 6+2+2 has three periods; 7+2 totals only 9.
options: One 7-hour period and one 2-hour period
Two 5-hour rest periods
One 6-hour period and two 2-hour periods
One 6-hour rest period and one 4-hour rest period
